narrator.name: Gradients (SN56)
narrator.role: Subnet team: competitive AutoML fine-tuning on Bittensor subnet 56
narrator.one_line: Rayon Labs' fine-tuning subnet, which frames itself as a tournament where miners race for hyperparameters and describes Bittensor as a marketplace whose incentives beat centralised AutoML.

statements.quote: Current AutoML platforms leave substantial performance untapped. Testing 180 fine-tuning tasks across models from 70M to 70B parameters, we found that HuggingFace AutoTrain, TogetherAI, Databricks, and Google Cloud consistently produce suboptimal configurations.
statements.context: Opening of the abstract of Rayon Labs' Gradients paper by Christopher Subia-Waud, setting the competitors it benchmarks against.

source.title: Gradients: When Markets Meet Fine-tuning - A Distributed Approach to Model Optimisation

statements.quote: Gradients, built on the Bittensor network, attacks this problem through competition. Independent miners race to find optimal hyperparameters, earning rewards proportional to their models' performance. This tournament drives exploration of configuration spaces that single-strategy methods never examine.
statements.context: Abstract of the Gradients paper describing the subnet mechanism.

source.title: Gradients: When Markets Meet Fine-tuning - A Distributed Approach to Model Optimisation

statements.quote: These findings demonstrate that decentralized systems with economic incentives can systematically outperform traditional AutoML, suggesting market dynamics may be key to achieving superior fine-tuning results.
statements.context: Closing sentence of the Gradients paper abstract, generalising from the subnet to decentralised systems.

source.title: Gradients: When Markets Meet Fine-tuning - A Distributed Approach to Model Optimisation

statements.quote: Built on the Bittensor network, it creates a marketplace where independent miners compete to find optimal configurations.
statements.context: Introduction of the Gradients paper describing what the Bittensor network provides.

source.title: Gradients: When Markets Meet Fine-tuning - A Distributed Approach to Model Optimisation

statements.quote: When miners profit from finding better configurations, they develop novel optimization techniques, share successful strategies within their organizations, and continuously refine their approaches.
statements.context: Discussion section of the Gradients paper on why competition beats a single algorithm.

source.title: Gradients: When Markets Meet Fine-tuning - A Distributed Approach to Model Optimisation

statements.quote: This suggests a fundamental shift in how we approach AutoML: from better algorithms to better incentive structures.

statements.quote: G.O.D is the subnet runtime behind Gradients.io training jobs and tournaments. Validators create tasks, coordinate miner and trainer infrastructure, evaluate results, and set weights. Miners expose training repositories for tournament tasks; trainers run those repositories on validator-controlled GPU infrastructure.
statements.context: The README of the rayonlabs/G.O.D repository, read in September 2026.

statements.quote: Tournaments are recurring competitions where miners submit open-source training code.
statements.context: The G.O.D README describing how the subnet runs.

foundation.mission.summary: Gradients says it exists to make fine-tuning better through competition and to let anyone train a model with no knowledge.

foundation.vision.summary: The paper's conclusion is a shift in AutoML from better algorithms to better incentive structures.

foundation.values.summary: Winning training code is open source and published.

problem.market.summary: Commercial AutoML platforms leave performance untapped and produce suboptimal configurations.

audience.summary: Two audiences: people with no training knowledge who want a model, and miners who profit from finding better configurations.

positioning.category.summary: An AutoML platform powered by a subnet; the network beneath it is a marketplace.

positioning.differentiator.summary: Competition among independent miners explores what single-strategy methods never examine.

positioning.reason.summary: Reason to believe is the 180-experiment benchmark and the claim that incentives make miners keep refining.

positioning.against.summary: Named opponents are HuggingFace AutoTrain, TogetherAI, Databricks and Google Cloud.

value.functional.summary: A few clicks and your model is trained, with higher accuracy on domain tasks.

value.self_expressive.summary: Anyone can train on Bittensor: joining means being a trainer without credentials.

messaging.h1.summary: Two repeated lines: the world's best AutoML platform, and anyone can train AI on Bittensor.

relationship.summary: The site says the platform is powered by subnet 56; the team speaks as builders of a product on top of a subnet.

language.term.summary: G.O.D, Gradients on Demand, names the subnet runtime; tournaments and trainers are its own vocabulary.

subnet.self.summary: Gradients describes itself as a tournament and a race among miners, and as the easiest place in the world to train a model.

subnet.network.summary: Bittensor is a marketplace and a decentralised system with economic incentives; the paper generalises the subnet's result to market dynamics, which is closer to Steeves's market language than to the foundation's.

coinages.meaning: the subnet runtime behind Gradients.io training jobs and tournaments

genealogy.summary: The June 2025 paper is the fullest statement: Gradients attacks AutoML through competition, miners race and are paid in proportion to performance [sn56-002], the Bittensor network is a marketplace [sn56-004], and the conclusion generalises to market dynamics and incentive structures [sn56-003] [sn56-006].
The 2026 site and README keep the tournament frame [sn56-012] [sn56-011] but the public pitch is accessibility: a few clicks, no knowledge needed [sn56-008], anyone can train on Bittensor [sn56-010].
genealogy.shift: from market proof to consumer accessibility

relations.note: The marketplace-of-miners frame echoes Steeves's market for intelligence
Same lab, same 'powered by Bittensor subnet' relationship wording
